Simulate Posterior Predictive Responses

Source: R/bayes_scale_simulate.R
simulate.multiScaleR_bayes.Rd

Generate replicate responses for fitted or new observations. Each replicate includes joint parameter uncertainty, any requested new-group effects, and the scatter of individual observations around their means, so replicates show the values you might record.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_bayes'
simulate(
  object,
  nsim = 1L,
  seed = NULL,
  newdata = NULL,
  kernel_inputs = NULL,
  row_id = NULL,
  re.form = NULL,
  scale_re.form = NULL,
  new_scale_levels = c("error", "sample", "zero"),
  new_response_levels = c("error", "sample", "zero"),
  trials = NULL,
  include_fixed = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A fitted multiScale_bayes() object with posterior draws, from sampling or either approximation.

nsim

Positive integer number of replicate data sets; default 1.

seed

Optional positive integer simulation seed. Your own random-number state is restored after simulation, even when it fails.

newdata

NULL (default) uses the fitted observations. Otherwise a nonempty data frame of new observations that holds the fixed covariates, the offset variables, and the grouping variables of every component you include. Response values are neither needed nor used.

kernel_inputs

Prepared landscape inputs for newdata, from kernel_prep() or kernel_prep_by_group(). Required with new data and NULL otherwise. Use the fitted kernel, predictor definitions, and physical map units. See "Match new rows to their landscapes" in predict.multiScaleR_bayes().

row_id

Name of the column in newdata that matches each row to an entry of kernel_inputs$binned$point_ids, or to a row name of kernel_inputs$kernel_dat for surface-only inputs. IDs may repeat. The default NULL uses the fitted row-ID column when the fit kept it, and the row names of newdata otherwise. Supply it for fits saved by older versions of the package. Used only with new data.

re.form

NULL (default) includes the response random effects. NA sets them all to zero while keeping group-specific scales. This is a reference prediction, not an average over the random effects.

scale_re.form

NULL (default) includes the fitted scale random effects and any sampled new ones. NA sets every scale deviation to zero. It is separate from re.form, which controls response effects.

new_scale_levels, new_response_levels

What to do with a group level that was not in the fitted data, set separately for scale and response random effects. "error" (default) stops, "sample" draws a new effect, and "zero" sets the new effect to zero. A sampled effect is one standard-normal value per new group and posterior draw, multiplied by that draw's group SD, and shared by every row in the group. Zeroing gives a typical-group reference, not a population average. Known groups keep their fitted effects. Neither choice creates a coefficient for a new level of a fixed factor.

trials

Positive integer binomial trial totals, one value or one per observation row. The default NULL keeps the fitted totals when you simulate the fitted rows. For new observations it uses one trial for a binary fit, and it is an error for a grouped binomial fit, which needs explicit totals. Use only with binomial models. Response columns in newdata never supply the totals.

include_fixed

Logical. With new data, TRUE recomputes declared fixed-radius landscape predictors from kernel_inputs, using their original preparation means and SDs. The default FALSE requires those columns in newdata. Source, metric, radius, kernel, and resolution must match the fitted preparation, including its max_D buffer extent. This adds no scale parameters or uncertainty.

...

Not used. Supplying any further argument is an error.

Value

A data frame with one row per fitted or new observation and one column per replicate data set, named sim_1, sim_2, and so on. Values are counts for Poisson and NB2 models, success counts out of the fitted or supplied trial totals for binomial models (not proportions), and response units for Gaussian models. Each column uses one complete posterior vector, drawn at random with replacement, together with the requested random effects.

For new data, a point_ids attribute gives the prepared landscape ID of each row, and a new_groups attribute lists the unseen levels that were sampled or set to zero, as in predict(). A prediction_contract attribute (see prediction_contract) marks the result as posterior predictive replicates that include observation noise and records the policies for included effects. It does not establish diagnostic eligibility or calibration.

Check the model against the data

Compare summaries of the replicate data sets with the same summaries of the observed response. An observed value far outside the replicated range means the model cannot reproduce that feature. Good sampling diagnostics do not show that the observation model fits the data, and agreement on one statistic does not establish adequacy. vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR") works through such a check. To use bayesplot, convert the replicates to a matrix with one simulated data set per row, t(as.matrix(replicated)). For a count model, ppc_stat() with stat = function(y) mean(y == 0) checks the fraction of zeros.

Simulate new groups jointly

Within one call, new-group effects are drawn afresh for each replicate data set and shared by all of its rows in that group. Different new groups are independent given the population parameters, whose joint posterior dependence is kept. Observation noise is then drawn separately for each row. Separate calls do not share a realization across components or batches, so put every row that enters a joint question into one call. Reusing a seed across predict_scales(), predict(), and simulate() does not promise matching latent effects, because the three functions use their random numbers differently.

To get an interval for a total, sum each replicate column first with colSums() and then take quantiles of the sums. Adding the limits of individual intervals overstates the range of the total.

The three prediction functions return different orientations, which matters for joint contrasts and totals. simulate() returns observations by replicates. predict(summary = FALSE) returns posterior draws by observations, and predict_scales(summary = FALSE) returns a named list of draws-by-observations matrices, one per landscape predictor.

Supply trials for binomial data

For a binary fit, new observations default to one trial. For a fit to cbind(successes, failures), supply the actual future totals, for example trials = rep(10L, nrow(newdata)). simulate() then returns success counts out of those totals, while predict() returns success probabilities whatever the number of trials.

See also

multiScale_bayes(), simulate_bayes_prior(), predict.multiScaleR_bayes(), predict_scales(), prediction_contract, multiScaleR_bayes; vignette("v14-bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR").

Examples

example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-annual-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
replicated <- simulate(example$fits$pooled, nsim = 20, seed = 94)
dim(replicated)  # one row per original observation, one column per replicate
#> [1] 100  20

# Posterior predictive check of the fraction of zero counts
range(vapply(replicated, function(y) mean(y == 0), numeric(1)))
#> [1] 0.00 0.04
mean(example$data$count == 0)  # observed fraction of zero counts
#> [1] 0.04
# These replicate counts include observation noise. Fitted means do not.

# Counts at eight future surveys, and an interval for their total
forecast <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-prediction-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
future <- simulate(forecast$fit, nsim = 200, seed = 803,
  newdata = forecast$newdata, kernel_inputs = forecast$kernel_inputs,
  row_id = "site_year", new_scale_levels = "sample",
  new_response_levels = "sample")
quantile(colSums(future), c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))  # total of the eight surveys
#>    2.5%     50%   97.5% 
#>  45.925  84.500 161.025
